title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
rawText:
When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.
But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.
This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.
“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”
The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.
The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.
The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.
Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”
Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.
Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.
“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”
For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.
Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”
The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.
Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.
“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.

title: Árbitro vendido y corrupto
rawText:
La peor noticia para una democracia no es que un partido se enquiste en el poder, sino que la ciudadanía deje de confiar en quien organiza las elecciones y cuente los votos. Tal como sucedía en el siglo pasado, cuando el organismo electoral dependía de la Secretaría de Gobernación.
Ese es el verdadero problema que enfrenta el Instituto Nacional Electoral rumbo a las elecciones intermedias de 2027.
Durante años, Morena y Andrés Manuel López Obrador emprendieron una ofensiva política contra el INE bajo el argumento de que era un organismo oneroso, burocrático y vinculado con los intereses del antiguo régimen. Después vinieron reformas, recortes presupuestales, confrontaciones y una recomposición de su Consejo General.
Hoy Guadalupe Taddei preside un instituto muy distinto al que encabezaron Lorenzo Córdova, Leonardo Valdés, Luis Carlos Ugalde o José Woldenberg.
A las controversias políticas se agregan además cuestionamientos administrativos sobre contrataciones realizadas durante la presidencia de Taddei.
Una investigación publicada esta semana por Reforma refiere controversias relacionadas con proveedores, adjudicaciones y el nombramiento de Jesús Octavio García González como director de Administración del instituto, quien posteriormente dejó el cargo tras una denuncia por posible conflicto de interés. Menciona el citado diario que la Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera de la SHCP tiene sitiado al INE.
Ante las denuncias de corrupción en el Instituto Nacional Electoral, seguramente el gobierno de la 4T dará carpetazo al asunto, sin considerar que el golpe será a la democracia, pero eso qué importa si lo que se trata es de eliminarla.
El INE maneja miles de millones de pesos, pero administra algo todavía más importante: la confianza electoral de los mexicanos y, cuando está en entredicho, pues se vislumbra que el abstencionismo sea el ganador en las elecciones intermedias del próximo año.
El costo de la democracia es oneroso y se observa en el tamaño del presupuesto del INE para el próximo año. El Consejo General aprobó un anteproyecto presupuestal por 31 mil 431 millones 887 mil 800 pesos para 2027, además de 10 mil 842 millones de pesos correspondientes al financiamiento público de partidos políticos y candidaturas independientes.
El propio instituto calcula que la Lista Nominal crecerá de aproximadamente 98 millones a más de 102 millones de ciudadanos y que deberán instalarse alrededor de 176 mil casillas, además de contratar aproximadamente 51 mil supervisores, capacitadores y asistentes electorales.
El INE deberá fiscalizar campañas, vigilar prerrogativas, monitorear radio y televisión, sancionar infracciones y tomar decisiones que inevitablemente beneficiarán a unos actores políticos y perjudicarán a otros.
Para ejercer semejante autoridad necesita algo que no puede comprarse con presupuesto público: credibilidad.
La autonomía tampoco consiste solamente en que la Constitución lo diga. Se demuestra todos los días manteniendo distancia del Ejecutivo, de los partidos políticos y de cualquier ente que pretenda mellar su independencia.
El árbitro no puede vestir ninguna camiseta.
Por eso sería un grave error que Morena considerara al INE como territorio conquistado, e igual de malo que algún consejero se despache con la cuchara grande en el manejo del presupuesto.
Cada licitación cuestionada debe aclararse. Cada adjudicación directa debe justificarse. Cada posible conflicto de interés debe investigarse. Cada nombramiento relevante debe sustentarse profesionalmente. Y cada resolución electoral debe poder defenderse jurídicamente sin necesidad de recurrir a afinidades políticas.
La elección de 2027 será suficientemente complicada por sí misma.
Habrá renovación de la Cámara de Diputados, elecciones locales y 17 gubernaturas en disputa. El propio INE reconoce que deberá enfrentar una operación electoral extraordinariamente amplia y costosa.
Ante este escenario, se equivocan el gobierno y el propio INE, ya que en lugar de ganar la confianza ciudadana para fortalecer el sistema electoral mexicano, se dedican a aceitar la maquinaria para pavimentar la victoria del oficialismo en las elecciones del 2027.
Tanto el PAN, de Jorge Romero; el PRI, de Alito Moreno; MC, de Dante Delgado, y Somos deberían avocarse para que el INE se despoje del sospechosismo que prevalece en torno a su autonomía e independencia del gobierno federal, porque de no hacerlo, en realidad serán tiempo y dinero perdido las campañas políticas y la lucha por el voto que se verá reflejado el día de la elección.

title: Trump rallying with Hinson in Iowa as she pledges to push back on White House
rawText:
Trump rallying with Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson in Iowa as she pledges to push back on White House
Sioux City, Iowa — President Trump is set to rally Thursday with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost Republican candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting modest pushback from the very candidates he's supporting.
Hinson, who is running for Iowa's open Senate seat, initially pledged to be the president's "top ally" in the upper chamber. But as she faces off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a contest that, like several in the Hawkeye State, has grown more competitive than expected, she's adjusted that commitment in recent weeks.
When she and Turek went head-to-head at a debate earlier this month, the former local news anchor said she would be Mr. Trump's ally when it's "important for Iowa." But she said she would "push back on him" when it's needed — as she said she would regardless of who's in the White House.
Last week, Hinson told Fox News: "If he's going to say something that's wrong, I'm going to challenge him on it."
"I'm not afraid to say, 'hey, I disagree with you on this,'" she said. "But I'll be an ally to somebody when they're with me."
For Republicans, the Senate race in Iowa is just one of several in which Democrats appear competitive despite Mr. Trump winning the state by double digits in 2024. Iowa has been hit hard by high energy prices and last year's U.S.-China trade war, which led Beijing to boycott American soybeans. It's a picture that appeared unthinkable at the outset of the cycle — and puts Republicans' Senate majority on the line.
Hinson, who's represented the state in the House since 2021, said she would be at the rally on Thursday to welcome Mr. Trump to Iowa, "because I think this is a contrast election."
As the nation experiences challenges, she posed the question: Who do Iowans want at the helm?
"You want a mom, a minivan-driving mom who's common sense, who's driving that common sense back into Washington, D.C.," she said. "I think that's what Iowans want as their U.S. senator."
Hinson has made the minivan motif central to her campaign. She connected the image to her emphasis on working with Mr. Trump for Iowans earlier this week, describing a recent call with the president.
"I had just finished dropping off the boys, I was ready to run an errand," Hinson said at an event in Des Moines geared toward moms, alongside Sen. Katie Britt. "And I see pop up on my caller ID in my minivan, 'DJT.'"
She continued, "'Ashley, it's your favorite president,' that's how he introduced himself."
Hinson said the call lasted five minutes and that Mr. Trump was "just checking in on us here in Iowa." She said she thanked the president for his efforts to move forward on trade with China and asked about a deal for China to buy more soybeans.
At the event, Hinson also delivered her latest break with the president, according to Semafor, telling reporters, "I don't think we need to be making any more deals with Russia," regarding Mr. Trump's waiver of sanctions against Moscow.
The criticism follows Hinson's move to separate herself from the president's handling of the war with Iran late last month. Tucked within a post expressing support for methods to combat high prices, such as a pause on diesel exports, Hinson made one of the first splits by a GOP Senate candidate with the president over the war, writing: "The war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."
The statement appeared in contrast to Hinson's vote earlier in September, when the House considered a resolution aimed at reining in the president in Iran. While two other Iowa Republicans locked in tight races supported the resolution, Hinson opposed it.
At the debate a couple weeks later, Turek pressed Hinson over those votes, saying during a discussion on energy costs: "We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran that Ashley Hinson voted in favor of continuing."
Hinson clarified during the debate that she believes the war must be brought to an "immediate and successful end" by not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon and by making sure that U.S. allies in the region are protected. Asked why she doesn't support the efforts to pass war powers resolutions in Congress, Hinson said, "I don't think we need another resolution."
"And I certainly don't want to see the president not be able to do a orderly end to this war," she added.
Thursday's rally marks the president's second visit to Iowa this year, after he kicked off campaigning in the midterms with a trip to the Des Moines area in January. Mr. Trump also announced plans last month for the largest steel plant in U.S. history to be built in Iowa, in an Oval Office event with Hinson in attendance. During the announcement, the president pledged to visit the state for a "great rally" to help get the Republican candidates elected.
"We'll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir," Hinson replied.

title: ¿Latinos le dan la espalda a Trump?
rawText:
En las elecciones de 2024 que trajeron de vuelta a Donald Trump a la Casa Blanca, uno de los resultados más sorpresivos y una de las narrativas más destacadas por los Republicanos fue la capitalización del voto latino. No fue un dato menor, pues el 46% de este sector votó rojo, frente a un 27-32% de las elecciones de 2020. Sin embargo, a menos de dos semanas de las elecciones de medio término, el mapa ha cambiado, mostrando que Trump pudo haber ganado votos, pero no aseguró lealtades.
Las últimas encuestan muestran que el partido del presidente llega debilitado entre los latinos a comparación del impulso del 2024. Según cifras del Pew Research Center, la intención de voto para la Cámara muestra una preferencia del 51% por el partido demócrata frente a un 24% al republicano. En este espectro, destaca la amplitud porcentual de personas que no eligieron a uno u a otro. Así mismo, de los latinos que votaron por Trump en 2024, el 65% indica que apoyaría al partido del presidente en las elecciones de la Cámara. Visto en términos proporcionales, aún se conserva una buena parte del núcleo. Sin embargo, surge la duda de si será suficiente. A esto se suma evaluaciones del desempeño de Donald Trump que oscilan entre el 27 y el 31%.
Al igual que está ocurriendo en una gran parte de las elecciones en el mundo, particularmente en América Latina, el electorado está marcando dos tendencias: el voto anti oficialismo y el voto definido por el costo de vida. En Estados Unidos no es la excepción, aunado a la “maldición de medio término” en donde el partido del presidente históricamente ha perdido terreno en las votaciones intermedias.
En este panorama, los altos precios de alimentos, vivienda y energía no desaparecieron con el cambio de presidente. En 2024, los latinos le daban a Trump una ventaja de cuatro puntos sobre Harris en el manejo de la economía. Hoy, les dan a los demócratas una ventaja de 21 puntos en ese tema. Casi dos tercios mencionan a NBC News/Telemundo que sus ingresos se están quedando cortos frente al costo de vida, en una proporción prácticamente idéntica a la de 2024. Esto pone en evidencia que la elección no implica una transformación ideológica, pero sí un castigo al oficialismo.
Adicionalmente, está el viraje respecto a la migración. Una de las grandes narrativas que se destacaron hace dos años fue esta idea de que los los latinos votaron en contra de sí mismos. Sin embargo, ahora esos latinos que apoyaron a Trump han cambiado de postura respecto a sus políticas migratorias, con al menos 67% de ellos alegando un exceso en las prácticas del ICE. Incluso entre los latinos que votaron por Trump, el Pew Reseacrh Center destaca que el 30% considera que se ha ido demasiado lejos particularmente en cuanto a deportaciones. Si bien en principio apoyaban una gestión fronteriza más ordenada y mayores controles, están rechazando su implementación.
Dentro de estos cambios, quizás lo más significativo, no solamente para estas elecciones sino para el futuro de la democracia estadounidense, es que este descontento no implica que haya un entusiasmo particular por los demócratas. Al igual que ocurre en otras latitudes, este partido no ha logrado consolidar una oposición sólida, padeciendo una evidente crisis de liderazgos fuertes, salvo contadas excepciones como el caso de Alaska, en donde el tradicional estado rojo podría cambiar de color el próximo 3 de noviembre. Esto implica que pueden recuperar votos, pero el descontento y la desconfianza siguen latentes.
De igual forma vale la pena destacar que Trump finalmente logró hacer la elección sobre su figura, pero no le está resultando como quería. Entre los latinos al menos, su nombre está generando más rechazo que convocatoria. Al menos 55% de los latinos registrados considera su voto para el Congreso como un voto contra Trump.
Aún está por verse los efectos de estas tendencias pues, como es sabido, las encuestas no son votos. Es importante destacar también que hay una porción significativa de votantes de este grupo demográfico que considera no ir a votar presencialmente precisamente por temor a que estén a la espera autoridades migratorias. Lo que es un hecho es que su presencia en las urnas puede hacer la diferencia en estados reñidos. Entre el segundo grupo demográfico más grande del país, queda claro que ambos partidos compiten por una lealtad que ninguno posee.

title: U.S. reducing troop footprint in Middle East, sources say
rawText:
Iran War Updates: U.S. reduces troop footprint in Mideast as indirect talks with Iran continue
What to know about the Iran war today:
- The U.S. military has quietly reduced its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats and attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, sources told CBS News on Wednesday. The latest attack, on King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi city of Dammam, has killed at least two people and injured eight more.
- Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. The IRGC said three other vessels hit sea mines and were forced to halt.
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue over a seven-day ceasefire proposal that President Trump initially rejected last month, with the U.S. seeking new clauses.
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a drone over Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen's escalating civil war said Thursday that it had intercepted another drone over the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the interception in a social media post, without offering further details.
Saudi Arabia has been pummeled by Houthi strikes in recent weeks. Experts say geography, missile interceptor shortages and evolving Houthi tactics are helping the Iranian proxy menace the kingdom, and global energy supplies.
Crude oil prices jump as Iran claims to have hit 7 tankers near Strait of Hormuz
World shares and U.S. futures retreated Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2% following a report by Iran's state television that seven oil tankers were hit by its military or sea mines and damaged near the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
If the claim by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the Gulf in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.
Brent crude, the international standard, gained 3.2% to hit $112.27 per barrel Thursday. It has been bouncing around $110 in recent days amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran might ease to allow the global energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal.
U.S. benchmark crude rose 2.8% to $99.80 per barrel.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX shed 1.1% to 25,367.96, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 1.3% to 7,816.67. Britain's FTSE 100 was down 0.7% at 10,678.67.
The future for the S&P 500 lost 1% and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was 0.7% lower.
CBS/AP
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it hit 4 vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in Persian Gulf
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. Ship-to-ship cargo transfers have become more common as tankers and other commercial vessels try to avoid Iranian detection and strikes in the strategic waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it "monitored and pursued four violating vessels that had previously passed through an illegal route," referring to shipping lanes in the strait that the Trump administration has encouraged vessels to use to avoid Iranian fees and controls. Tehran considers those southern routes, close to Oman's coast, unauthorized and has targeted vessels trying to use them for months.
"They discovered the vessels transferring oil cargoes from ship to ship in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf," the bulletin read. "All four ships were hit simultaneously and are burning."
The IRGC said three other ships attempting to use routes not recognized by Iran "suffered accidents and caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and were brought to a halt."
The IRGC said the U.S. "encouraging vessels to pass through an illegally mined passage has led to an increasing number of maritime incidents day by day."
"If this course continues," the group warned, "the confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region."
Saudi authorities raise death toll in attack on airport in eastern city of Dammam to 2
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Thursday that the latest attack on the kingdom's airports, a strike on the eastern city of Dammam's King Fahd International Airport, had risen to two.
"The number of deaths resulting from the attack has risen to two, after confirming an additional death. The deceased were a Saudi citizen and a resident of Indian nationality," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement shared on social media.
It said eight others, "a Saudi citizen, two residents each of Indian, Yemeni, and Bangladeshi nationalities, and a resident of Nepalese nationality," were injured in the attack.
The statement did not assign blame for the attack, but Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have attacked Saudi airports and other infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the Saudi government's backing of Yemeni state forces in the neighboring nation's decade-long civil war.
GACA said in its statement that it was continuing work in conjunction with other security authorities "to assess the damages, and to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and employees, and to maintain the security and safety of the civil aviation system in the Kingdom."
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom and prompted the U.S. to quietly reduce its military footprint in the region as missiles hit energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing more than 20 people.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels.

title: "Dejé secretos de Estado en el tren; soy la prueba de que es posible recuperarse del mayor error de tu vida"
rawText:
"Dejé secretos de Estado en el tren; soy la prueba de que es posible recuperarse del mayor error de tu vida"
  - Autor, Jennifer Meierhans
  - Título del autor, BBC News
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 6 min
Advertencia: esta historia contiene una referencia al suicidio.
Richard Jackson cometió el mayor error de su vida un martes cualquiera, cuando iba en el tren de camino al trabajo.
El funcionario británico olvidó documentos altamente clasificados en el tren. Cuando se dio cuenta, presa del pánico, ya era demasiado tarde.
El error, cometido en una fracción de segundo, se convirtió en noticia nacional en Reino Unido y la vida de Jackson se vio sumida en el caos.
Se sintió consumido por la vergüenza y la humillación.
Casi 20 años después, relata aquel fatídico día y sus consecuencias en una entrevista con la doctora Sian Williams para el pódcast Life Changing de BBC Radio 4.
Jackson dice ser la prueba de que, incluso tras cometer el peor error, es posible reconstruir la vida.
Antes de que todo se desmoronara, Jackson tenía 37 años y vivía en Yateley, en el sur de Reino Unido, con su esposa, Maddie, y su hijastra Charlotte, de 15 años.
Su otra hijastra, Becky, de 20 años, estaba en la universidad.
"Éramos muy felices", recuerda. "Pero yo estaba muy centrado en mi carrera".
"Mi valía y mi valor provenían de esa carrera, ese puesto, esa posición y esa responsabilidad", cuenta.
"Durante un tiempo, llegué a trabajar 100 horas semanales. No desconectaba".
Jackson había sido transferido por el Ministerio de Defensa británico a la Oficina del Gabinete para un puesto relacionado con el terrorismo global, donde manejaba información de primera mano procedente del GCHQ, el MI5 y el MI6; es decir, los servicios de inteligencia británicos.
Al salir de su oficina en Whitehall un lunes por la tarde, recogió una pila de formularios que debía llenar para formalizar su comisión de servicio.
De vuelta en casa, se dio cuenta de que, entre el paquete, había "dos documentos sobre dos temas clasificados y ambos eran ultrasecretos".
"Nadie más lo sabrá"
En retrospectiva, Jackson dice que debería haber llamado a la Oficina del Gabinete y haber pedido a alguien que recogiera los documentos de forma segura.
Pero atribuye lo que hizo después a "cierto instinto de supervivencia".
"Quizá si los devuelvo, nadie lo sabrá nunca".
Jackson guardó los documentos ultrasecretos en una carpeta de cartón de color naranja brillante y, a la mañana siguiente, se sentó en el tren pensando una y otra vez: "No olvides esto".
Bajó del tren y caminó a paso ligero hacia Whitehall. Entonces se dio cuenta de que no tenía la carpeta... "Por un instante, sentí como si el mundo se hubiera detenido".
Jackson fue a todas las estaciones donde paraba el tren y preguntó si alguien había entregado una carpeta. Nada.
"Estaba desesperado. Todo, cada movimiento, se sentía muy brusco... Me sentía mal".
No se derrumbó hasta que vio a Maddie, su esposa.
"Le dije que había arruinado nuestras vidas. Ella simplemente me abrazó. Me dijo que todo estaría bien y que saldríamos adelante".
En manos de la BBC
Al día siguiente, en el trabajo, Jackson descubrió que los documentos habían sido encontrados y entregados a la BBC.
Jackson relata que su primera sensación fue de "alivio al saber que los documentos estaban de vuelta en un lugar seguro", antes de darse cuenta de que "iban a ser públicos".
"Fui la noticia principal del informativo de las 6 de la tarde. Y me suspendieron a la espera de una investigación".
Jackson se escondió en casa. Un mediodía, Maddie lo encontró sentado con las piernas cruzadas en el sofá, sollozando.
"Pasé la mañana tratando de encontrar una forma indolora de morir", dice. "A menudo he pensado qué habría pasado si ella no hubiera vuelto a casa ese mediodía... pero supongo que nunca lo sabré".
Y prosigue: "Pasamos esa tarde hablando. Y creo que fue la primera vez que pensé: 'Si quiero superar esto, no puedo hacerlo solo'".
La Oficina del Gabinete consideró que se trataba de una falta grave y lo bajó de categoría tres grados. Fue acusado según la Ley de Secretos Oficiales, evitó la cárcel y fue multado con 2.500 libras esterlinas (más de US$3.300).
En teoría, todo había terminado. Pero Jackson no podía librarse de la vergüenza, el arrepentimiento y la humillación.
Agradece a las muchas personas que se preocuparon por él y lo ayudaron a reconstruir su vida.
"Yo mismo arreglé muy poco. Mucha gente me ayudó a arreglar las cosas".
Tras regresar al Ministerio de Defensa en un puesto de recursos humanos y pasar al Departamento de Cultura, Medios de Comunicación y Deporte para trabajar en los Juegos Olímpicos, Jackson dejó la administración pública y trabajó para los Samaritanos.
Posteriormente asumió la dirección de un equipo de analistas que estudiaban el riesgo del terrorismo global y, en su tiempo libre, comenzó a formarse como coach de desarrollo personal.

title: La traidora y la política
rawText:
El encuentro a puerta cerrada de hace unas semanas entre Claudia Sheinbaum y Maru Campos durante una gira de la presidenta por Chihuahua fue el espacio de negociación y acuerdos —secretos, confidenciales— donde se fraguó el fin de la confrontación.
El aciago episodio del operativo que involucró a agentes de la CIA en territorio mexicano había sido el ariete por medio del cual la presidenta había golpeado insistentemente a la gobernadora.
Campos había solicitado múltiples audiencias con la presidenta en Palacio, que le habían sido denegadas.
Aprovechando su gira por el estado, la presidenta cedió, se reunió con ella y encontraron puntos de acuerdo.
La gobernadora tiró bajo el ferrocarril a su aliado, colaborador y exfiscal César Jáuregui, depositando en él toda la responsabilidad del operativo que, por cierto, terminó en tragedia, con la muerte accidental —se dice— de los dos agentes al desbarrancarse el vehículo en el que regresaban después de haber desmantelado el laboratorio de drogas.
Maru Campos salvó el pellejo, la eventualidad de investigaciones posteriores y aplicó el pragmatismo político al entregar a un “culpable”, muy probablemente chivo expiatorio del incidente.
La presidenta negoció el cambio de narrativa, el fin de la reyerta y la persecución judicial del exfiscal, evidentemente panista. Hoy niega toda negociación, al afirmar que la justicia jamás está sujeta a acuerdos, pero las evidencias son aplastantes.
Desde el encuentro hubo un cambio de discurso en el mensaje de la presidenta. De la misma forma que Campos marcó distancia con su excolaborador y abrió supuestas carpetas de investigación en su contra.
Las previas, las existentes en torno al operativo, curiosamente, ni siquiera mencionan el nombre de Jáuregui. De la noche a la mañana, se le responsabilizó de la entrada de los agentes americanos a territorio nacional, lo que sustenta, dice el gobierno federal, el desproporcionado delito de traición a la patria.
Jáuregui se equivocó en la jerga de campaña por convertirse en presidente municipal de Chihuahua capital, al reconocer y asumir públicamente la responsabilidad por el operativo que incluyó a los agentes de la CIA. Su consideración pudiera sustentarse en la construcción de una imagen como exfiscal fuerte, sin miedo a atacar al crimen organizado.
Pero quedan sobre la mesa más preguntas que respuestas.
Es inverosímil pensar que la gobernadora no estuviera al tanto, que no le hubieran reportado el operativo que, como hoy pretende olvidar, ella misma defendió al principio como un instrumento de justicia y protección al pueblo de Chihuahua.
Hoy afirma lo contrario: no sabía, actuaron por su cuenta. ¿Por qué entonces no lo denunció y dijo así desde el principio?
Existe la borrosa figura del subprocurador que hoy se encuentra prófugo y que, al parecer, es la persona que en efecto coordinó y supervisó la entrada de los agentes, mientras su jefe Jáuregui, hoy preso en el Altiplano, trabajaba en su campaña.
Maru traicionó a su colaborador de muchos años, aliado e incluso amigo.
Lo hizo tal vez para asegurar que nadie la persiga al terminar su gobierno y, por qué no, tal vez recibir una generosa embajada extendida por la presidenta al estilo de su antecesor.
A los gobernadores que se cuadran frente al águila presidencial, que se alinean con la 4T, se les premia con la cancelación de cualquier carpeta de investigación por posibles ilícitos o conductas indebidas durante su administración, y de paso, la beca dorada de una embajada extranjera. Hay múltiples casos que lo demuestran.
La presidenta, por su parte, hizo lo que tantos otros en el pasado: negociar la justicia, como instrumento de poder y de control.
Se persigue, encarcela, acusa y enjuicia a los opositores, no a los militantes del fallido movimiento.
Se exhibe como delincuentes a los servidores y funcionarios de otros partidos, jamás a los morenistas, aunque la evidencia de ilícitos, cochupos, negocios, contratos y concesiones escapa por las oficinas públicas y los departamentos gubernamentales.
La justicia a modo, como hicieron los del PRI en su momento y también los del PAN.
Son lo mismo, utilizan el poder de la misma forma: la justicia sometida a los intereses partidistas.
La justicia y el poder al servicio del partido, no de los mexicanos.

title: Timbiriche: Sasha une los puntos
rawText:
“No puedes unir los puntos mirando hacia adelante; solo puedes unirlos mirando hacia atrás”, dijo Steve Jobs en 2005 ante los graduados de Stanford para decir que el sentido de algunas experiencias solo se revela con el tiempo. Lo que parece suelto o sin rumbo cobra significado cuando, años después, miramos atrás y entendemos cómo llegamos aquí.
Y justo eso hizo Sasha Sokol, integrante de Timbiriche, una banda cuyo nombre proviene de un juego de lápiz y papel que, curiosamente, consiste en unir puntos con líneas. Gana quien cierra el cuadro. A Sasha le tomó décadas unir los puntos de su historia hasta poder nombrarla: abuso.
Ella tenía 14 años; Luis de Llano, 39. Por años, la historia se contó como un romance de la farándula. Llamar amor al abuso forma parte de una cultura de la violación que la minimiza mediante prejuicios y termina responsabilizando a quien la sufre.
En junio de 2025, la Suprema Corte resolvió una demanda por daño moral en contra de Luis de Llano y estableció que no hay plazo para reclamar una reparación por violencia sexual sufrida durante la infancia. Reconoció que los tiempos de las víctimas no necesariamente coinciden con los legales: pueden pasar años antes de que una persona pueda nombrar lo que vivió y acudir a la justicia. La decisión no prohíbe contar esa historia, pero sí la recapitula y declara la conducta indebida del adulto.
La violencia contra las niñas sigue arraigada en nuestra cultura. Según CONAPO, en 2025 se estimaron 7 mil 887 nacimientos de madres de entre 10 y 14 años. Además, el 18.2% de las jóvenes reportó haberse unido en pareja antes de cumplir 18 años. Así, el matrimonio infantil está prohibido, pero las uniones tempranas persisten detrás de las condiciones sociales que empujan a las niñas a vivir como adultas.
La historia de Sasha vuelve a las pantallas. ViX estrenó una serie sobre Timbiriche, cuyo productor ha llamado al caso Sokol su “columna vertebral”. La pregunta es incómoda: ¿hasta dónde llega la libertad creativa cuando una obra recrea la violencia que sufrió una persona identificable durante su infancia?
Contar esta historia es legítimo, incluso necesario. La libertad de expresión protege también las narraciones incómodas y no exige, como regla general, autorización de sus protagonistas. Sin embargo, esa libertad no es absoluta: debe ponderarse frente a la dignidad, la vida privada y otros derechos de las personas retratadas. Que Sasha no haya participado en la producción no la vuelve ilícita por sí sola. No obstante, sí obliga a cuestionar cómo se cuenta su historia.
¿La presenta como una niña frente a un adulto con poder o reproduce la idea de que ella lo buscaba y, por tanto, era responsable? La sentencia de la Corte no resolvió esa discusión artística, pero sí desautorizó la lógica que traslada a una niña la responsabilidad del abuso. Esto es, a mi juicio, la serie reproduce una lógica incompatible con el reconocimiento judicial de la violencia sufrida por una niña.
La producción se escuda en una leyenda final en cada episodio. No basta. Un texto no deshace horas de narrativa que avala, o cuando menos matiza, el actuar del adulto. La advertencia no protege a Sasha; parece que pretende cubrir al abusador y a la libertad creativa.
Pero el problema no se reduce a Luis de Llano. Alcanza a la normalización de esa relación, a los medios que la contaron como una historia de amor y a una sociedad que todavía pregunta qué sentía una niña por un adulto, antes de indignarse por lo que ese adulto hacía con una niña.
No se trata de censurar ni de mermar la libertad creativa. Se trata de no disfrazar la violencia de amor. El punto de encuentro está en reconocer que la protección de las niñas también depende de las historias que contamos y cómo las contamos.
Sasha unió los puntos de su propia vida; nadie tiene derecho a trazar las líneas por ella. En el timbiriche gana quien cierra el cuadro. Sasha ya cerró el suyo en la Corte; ninguna serie debería volver a abrirlo.

Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.
"They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.
When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."
Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.
All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.
"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.
It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.
"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."
Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..
Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases. In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.
And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.
That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.
"If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."
This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.
Big picture
From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption.
That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.
All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.
"We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News. "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."
Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.
"She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."
In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.
Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.
"Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."
Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.
"I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.
How it plays
Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.
"As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.
He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.

title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
rawText:
Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.
Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.
At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall, a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.
"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."
Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.
Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.
Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.
"People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.
When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.
"After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."
Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.
Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.
Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.
In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.
"I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.
Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."
Solomon says this is a natural progression.
Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."
Research by NPR's Susie Cummings.

title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
rawText:
Chemical leak in Toledo forces hazardous materials evacuation, shelter-in-place orders
A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal.
One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital.
Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release.
In an update Wednesday, Toledo officials say the evacuation and shelter-in-place zone has been reduced to half a mile. The orders beyond that zone have been lifted.
"There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank."
The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday.
Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.
MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.
According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.
Who is in the evacuation zone?
According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:
- Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.
- Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.
The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported.
Toledo public schools were closed on Wednesday.

title: North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South
rawText:
Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.
The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.
Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music and news criticising Pyongyang.
If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.
At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.
The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.
Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.
The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.
The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.
Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.
North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

title: Teacher who survived Bend shooting tried to close door, ‘but the shooter was already there’
rawText:
A teacher who was shot by a teenage gunman in a Bend, Oregon, elementary school last week said she saw the attacker and tried to shut the classroom door, “but the shooter was already there.”
Becky Drury said she was shot at close range in the rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday.
“Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured,” Drury said in a statement Wednesday.
“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” she said. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”
Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher were killed in the attack, which began around 1 p.m., officials said.
The gunman was fatally shot by a bystander who saw him fire at a truck and enter the school, police have said. The bystander followed the 16-year-old gunman and shot him as another teacher was wrestling with him over the weapon, according to police.

title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
rawText:
Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.
On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.
During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”
Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”
The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”
Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.
Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.
Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able).
As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”
“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”
The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

title: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
rawText:
A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.
Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
New research out of Texas shows how data centers are driving up pollution.
New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.
Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”
In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.
That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.
NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.
Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

title: Airbnb limits chores for guests, sparking backlash from hosts
rawText:
Airbnb is taking steps to limit the chores that hosts can require of guests prior to checkout, addressing a long-standing grievance among customers who often pay cleaning fees and are told they must do a list of tasks themselves.
In a new policy update, Airbnb prohibits hosts from mandating that guests strip beds, wash and put away dishes, start laundry, or remove trash from the property. This new guideline will apply to reservations made on or after November 20.
This change comes in response to years of backlash regarding overly burdensome checkout instructions and hefty fines for not disposing of trash. Many guests have voiced their frustrations on social media, questioning why they should be responsible for cleaning tasks after already paying a cleaning fee.
However, some hosts aren’t pleased with the update. Within Airbnb’s community forums, some argue that basic cleaning responsibilities are essential for maintaining sanitary conditions and protecting their properties. They point out that hosts must manage the costs and practical demands of preparing their properties for the next guests.
One host expressed concern that the new policy leans toward a hotel-like model, which detracts from the unique appeal of Airbnb.
“Guests are given complete freedom to be lazy while the hosts bear the risk,” the host wrote. “The major distinction between commercial hotels and my private home is the personal touch. Guests can certainly be expected to wash their dishes or put them in the dishwasher and remove their dirty linens. In exchange, they enjoy a personal connection and a unique environment that a hotel simply can’t provide. Plus, every potential guest has the opportunity to read the listing beforehand and decide what they prefer. If these restrictions are removed, it could lead me to withdraw my listing and bid farewell to Airbnb after twelve years.”
Airbnb has outlined some exceptions to the new policy, though. Hosts may still ask guests to conserve water during droughts or use bear-proof trash containers in areas where wildlife poses a risk.
The policy change highlights the challenge Airbnb faces in balancing the expectations of guests versus hosts and is another step taken in addressing guests’ concerns. The company faced scrutiny in 2024 over price transparency from hosts tacking on cleaning fees after guests booked their listings. In 2023, the company said more than 260,000 hosts had reduced or eliminated their cleaning fees. In May 2025, Airbnb began displaying total prices — including fees but excluding taxes — by default in search results worldwide.
It will be interesting to see how many hosts decide the new restrictions make Airbnb less attractive as a platform. But the move could also draw in more travelers who want the convenience of a rental without feeling as though they are both paying for housecleaning while still expected to clean the home themselves.

title: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
rawText:
Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives. As part of its third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, the company says the non-voting stock will also go toward potential acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading beginning in 2027.
Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
Meta says the new class of shares will also fund acquisitions and employee compensation.
“The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.”
Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate.
It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.
Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

title: TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026: Everything you need to know

title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
rawText:
Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.
But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.
He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders.
“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.
Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.
Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.
Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.
Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales.
“On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.”
Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.
Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].”
“And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

title: Bukele pide la liberación de 4 soldados salvadoreños "secuestrados" en Haití por pandillas y dice que hay una operación militar para rescatarlos
rawText:
Bukele pide la liberación de 4 soldados salvadoreños "secuestrados" en Haití por pandillas y dice que hay una operación militar para rescatarlos
El presidente de El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, pidió este miércoles la liberación de cuatro soldados salvadoreños que llevan desaparecidos en Haití desde el domingo.
A los cuatro miembros de la Fuerza Aérea se les perdió el rastro tras una emboscada perpetrada por "grupos criminales fuertemente armados", según informaron las Fuerzas Armadas de El Salvador.
El equipo salvadoreño forma parte de la Fuerza de Represión de Pandillas (GSF, por su sigla en inglés), un cuerpo multinacional creado por el Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas en octubre de 2025 y cuya misión es restablecer la seguridad en Haití.
La emboscada ocurrió en Croix-des-Bouquets, una comunidad antes pacífica de Puerto Príncipe que ahora está controlada por grupos armados.
Según informa el diario salvadoreño La Prensa Gráfica, Bukele publicó el mensaje horas después que la GSF y la Policía Nacional de Haití confirmaran que realizan operativos en la zona donde fueron atacados los soldados salvadoreños y que debido a los enfrentamientos habían fallecido varios pandilleros.
Tras cuatro días sin referirse al incidente, en un mensaje compartido en la red social X, Bukele se dirigió directamente a quienes "tienen como rehenes" a los salvadoreños.
"Nuestros hombres secuestrados no son combatientes. Son técnicos de aviación que forman parte de nuestra misión en Haití, dentro del marco de una misión internacional. Nuestra misión consiste únicamente en pilotos y personal técnico, cuyo trabajo principal es realizar evacuaciones médicas y salvar vidas, no hacer la guerra", dice Bukele en su comunicado.
"Sin embargo, fueron secuestrados de manera cobarde mientras regresaban después de comprar alimentos en un mercado de la zona", prosigue.
"Por eso, hoy hemos lanzado una operación militar para rescatarlos. Tenemos un solo objetivo: traer de vuelta a nuestros cuatro compatriotas a casa con vida, sin ningún daño".
Bukele termina su mensaje con una advertencia, y recordando la política de seguridad con la que ha desarticulado a las pandillas en su país y que le ha valido una popularidad sin precedentes para un jefe de gobierno, además de críticas por violaciones de derechos humanos.
"Quiero que ustedes, los líderes de las pandillas, comprendan una cosa muy claramente: el ataque de hoy no es nada comparado con lo que se viene si no recuperamos a los cuatro rehenes con vida", escribió el mandatario.
"Ya acabamos con las pandillas en El Salvador, y también podemos acabar con ustedes".
En marzo de 2024 Bukele aseguró que su gobierno podía solucionar la creciente crisis de violencia de Haití y que solo necesitaría "una resolución del Consejo de Seguridad de la ONU, el consentimiento del país anfitrión y cubrir todos los gastos de la misión".
Control de pandillas
Los soldados salvadoreños fue atacado cuando regresaba al campamento en un vehículo blindado, según informaron las Fuerzas Armadas en un comunicado a última hora del domingo. Lograron huir después de que su vehículo fuera alcanzado por explosivos y se incendiara, pero a continuación se perdió el contacto.
Otros países que llevan a cabo operaciones contra las bandas en Haití intentaron prestar ayuda, mientras que los helicópteros salvadoreños desplegados para prestar apoyo fueron blanco de disparos.
"Se han realizado múltiples intentos de aproximación por vía terrestre y aérea, pero estos se han visto obstaculizados por la intensidad de los enfrentamientos y las condiciones de seguridad en la zona", afirmaron las FFAA de El Salvador.
Hasta el momento ninguna pandilla se ha atribuido el ataque.
Este es el primer ataque de esa naturaleza contra la fuerza internacional y ocurre en un momento en el que Haití se prepara para sus primeras elecciones generales en más de una década. Lo sucedido pone de relieve el poder de las pandillas armadas en Haití, que controlan aproximadamente el 70% de Puerto Príncipe, la capital.
Romain Le Cour, jefe del Observatorio de Haití en la Iniciativa Global contra el Crimen Organizado Transnacional, declaró el lunes que, si bien algunos grupos criminales han estado bajo presión desde que se desplegó la fuerza de supresión de pandillas, "otras quieren demostrar que pueden contraatacar".
"Si efectivamente estos soldados están retenidos, los grupos obtienen ventaja para negociar y para presionar a las fuerzas de seguridad", afirmó en unas declaraciones recogidas por la agencia de noticias Reuters.
El Consejo de Seguridad de la ONU autorizó en septiembre de 2025 una fuerza de supresión de pandillas de 5.550 integrantes a fin de reemplazar a una anterior fuerza multinacional liderada por Kenia, que tuvo dificultades por la falta de fondos y recursos en su intento por ayudar a la Policía Nacional de Haití a contener la violencia de las pandillas.
La fuerza de supresión de pandillas cuenta actualmente con más de 1.500 efectivos desplegados en el país caribeño, e incluye soldados de Chad, Jamaica y Guatemala.
La violencia de las pandillas ha desplazado a una cifra récord de 1,5 millones de personas en los últimos años en Haití, además de dejar más de 5.700 muertos y heridos desde enero hasta mediados de septiembre, y más de 230 personas secuestradas, según Naciones Unidas.
